prompt.context: Two entrepreneurs are launching a non-profit chocolate bar manufacturing company called Madecasse. The goal of Madecasse is to improve conditions for people in Madagascar by selling chocolate bars to consumers in the United States. Our firm is working with Madecasse on a pro-bono basis to determine two things: (1) where to source materials (Venezuela, Madagascar, Colombia) and (2) how to market the bars in the United States.
prompt.question: Where should Madecasse source its cocoa beans, and how should it market its chocolate bars to American consumers?

clarifying_info.q: What is the primary goal of Madecasse?
clarifying_info.a: The mission of Madecasse is to improve the economic welfare of people in Madagascar.

clarifying_info.q: Can Madecasse sell all the bars it produces?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume Madecasse will be able to sell as many chocolate bars as it makes.
Manufacturing will take place in the same location as the cocoa sourcing.

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about Madagascar?
clarifying_info.a: Population of 22M; Literacy: 70%; GDP/capita: $900; GDP is 30% agriculture; Population below poverty line: 50%; fairly stable government now, with a recent history of instability.

clarifying_info.q: What are the relative labor costs across sourcing options?
clarifying_info.a: Labor costs are highest in Venezuela and lowest in Madagascar. Venezuela employs more technology and harvests more rapidly. Fields yield more crops per hectare in Venezuela and least in Madagascar. Colombia has the most available land, Madagascar the least.

clarifying_info.q: What do we know about US consumers?
clarifying_info.a: Growing taste for dark chocolate; typically buy as impulse buys at grocery or convenience stores; generally willing to pay $2/bar; top 25% of income earners willing to pay more for high-end bars; growing tendency to pay more for items associated with a cause.
3 primary brands with multiple products; typically have ingredients outside chocolate (e.g., nuts, caramel); sold through grocery stores, convenience stores, and gas stations.

exhibits.title: Sourcing Comparison: Madagascar, Colombia, Venezuela
exhibits.shows: A table comparing three cocoa sourcing locations across pounds per hectare, available hectares, manhours to harvest a hectare, cost per manhour, bars per pound of beans, and price per bar.

framework: 1. Madagascar: Social (demographics, income distribution, family/culture), Political (stability, rule of law), Economic (industries, agriculture share)
2. Sourcing Options — compare Venezuela, Madagascar, Colombia on: climate for cocoa, crops per hectare, available land, technology use, infrastructure, fixed and variable costs
3. US Consumers: chocolate preferences (dark/milk, with or without nuts/fruit), willingness to pay for normal bar vs. cause-linked bar, average spend by demographic group
4. Distribution options: retail/grocery, online, specialty channels
5. Competitive landscape: number of other bars, current market share, marketing approach, product types
6. Other: export regulations, tariffs, environmental concerns

questions.prompt: What subjects would you consider in comparing the three sourcing locations?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: costs (labor, transportation, equipment), quality of cocoa, harvest size (yield per hectare x available land), export issues, tariffs, local government stability, and environmental concerns. The key insight is that the analysis must go beyond pure profit and consider impact on Madagascar's economy.

questions.prompt: [Give Exhibit 1] Which location should Madecasse source from, and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute total harvest, total labor costs, revenue, profit, and then assess 'impact to Madagascar' (defined as revenue generated in Madagascar). Greater profit is available from Colombia or Venezuela, but sourcing from Madagascar maximizes economic impact to Madagascar because all labor costs flow to local workers. The correct recommendation is Madagascar despite lower profit margins.

math.setup: For each location: Total Harvest (lbs) = Pounds/hectare x Available hectares. Total Manhours = Manhours/hectare x Available hectares. Total Labor Cost = Total Manhours x $/manhour. Bars = Total Harvest x Bars/pound. Revenue = Bars x Price/bar. Profit = Revenue - Labor Cost. Impact to Madagascar = Revenue if sourcing from Madagascar (labor + profit stays local), or just Labor Cost paid if sourcing elsewhere.
steps: Madagascar: Harvest = 3,000 x 12,500 = 37.5M lbs; Manhours = 6 x 12,500 = 75M hrs (wait: manhours per hectare=6, so total = 6 x 12,500 = 75,000? Re-check with exhibit solution: Total Manhours = 225M => 6 x 12,500 = 75,000 hectare-manhours; exhibit shows 225M meaning units are man-hours total including scale factor. Using exhibit solution numbers directly:
Madagascar: Total Harvest = 37.5M lbs; Total Labor Cost = $337.5M; Bars = 75M; Revenue = $375M; Profit = $37.5M; Impact to Madagascar = $375M (all revenue stays in Madagascar)
Colombia: Total Harvest = 100M lbs; Total Labor Cost = $875M; Bars = 200M; Revenue = $1,000M; Profit = $125M; Impact to Madagascar = $125M (only profit sent back, if any)
Venezuela: Total Harvest = 102M lbs; Total Labor Cost = $688.5M; Bars = 204M; Revenue = $1,020M; Profit = $331.5M; Impact to Madagascar = $331.5M
Conclusion: Madagascar sourcing yields the highest impact to Madagascar at $375M vs $331.5M (Venezuela) and $125M (Colombia), even though profit is lowest at $37.5M.
math.answer: Source from Madagascar. Impact to Madagascar = $375M (highest of the three options), even though absolute profit ($37.5M) is lowest. The mission of maximizing economic welfare in Madagascar is best served by sourcing locally.

brainstorming.prompt: What considerations should Madecasse take into account when selling bars to American consumers? Cover: (1) target demographic, (2) probable distribution channels, (3) how to position the bar vs. competitors.

categories.name: Target Demographic
ideas: Wealthier individuals (top 25% income) who tend toward high-end foods
Socially conscious consumers willing to pay a premium for cause-linked products
Dark chocolate enthusiasts given growing market trend
Urban consumers in high-income zip codes

categories.name: Distribution Channels
ideas: Higher-end grocery stores (e.g., Whole Foods, Trader Joe's)
Coffee shops and cafes as partners

categories.name: Positioning vs. Competitors
ideas: Lead with cause: proceeds improve economic welfare in Madagascar
Emphasize quality and single-origin cocoa story
Price at premium tier ($5/bar) above mass-market $2/bar
Simple, pure ingredients vs. competitors who add nuts/caramel
Transparent supply chain and social impact metrics
Packaging that tells the Madagascar story visually

recommendation: Madecasse should source its cocoa from Madagascar, which maximizes economic impact to Madagascar at $375M — higher than Colombia ($125M) or Venezuela ($331.5M) even though Madagascar produces lower absolute profit.

The chocolate bars should target wealthy American consumers (top 25% income earners) willing to pay a $5/bar premium, sold through high-end grocery stores, specialty retailers, and partnerships with coffee shops.
risks: Even wealthy consumers may not be willing to pay $5/bar, especially during a recession
A resurgence of political instability in Madagascar could disrupt sourcing and operations
Higher cost per bar ($4.50) leaves very thin margin ($0.50/bar) and no buffer for unexpected cost increases
Dependence on a single, geographically concentrated source creates supply chain vulnerability
next_steps: Interview consumers to test willingness to pay $5/bar for a cause-linked product
Identify and vet reliable cocoa suppliers in Madagascar
Develop partnerships with high-end grocery chains and coffee shops
Build marketing materials that communicate the Madagascar social impact story clearly
